strengths: Clear and practical problem: verifier-free test-time scaling for autoregressive VLAs, avoiding the training cost and generalization issues of external verifiers/value functions (Nakamoto et al., Kwok et al.).

The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: using KL divergence from a condition-masked (uncertainty-aware) reference distribution as a confidence signal, with a joint fine-tuning strategy (condition dropout) to make the reference distribution well-behaved. The connection to self-certainty methods in LLMs (Kang et al., 2025) is appropriately positioned.

Comprehensive evaluation across four settings (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, and real-robot Franka experiments) with two VLA architectures (π0-FAST, OpenVLA), covering in-distribution, OOD, and low-data regimes (30/100/300 demos). The 168% relative gain in the 30-demo RoboCasa regime is notable.

Thorough ablations covering inference strategy, number of candidates, masking variants, joint training, regularization temperature, and aggregation, plus an inference-latency analysis with a single-prefill deployment variant that makes the method practical (~23-30s regardless of N).
Good reproducibility: detailed training configurations, hyperparameter search ranges, and an LLM usage disclosure are provided.
weaknesses: Heavy per-dataset hyperparameter tuning with 'report the best result' (Appendix A.3): sampling temperature, N, masking variant, and regularization temperature are all searched per dataset and the best configuration reported. This raises concerns about evaluation fairness/overfitting to the test environments, and undermines the framing of the method as a simple, generally-applicable signal — the optimal masking variant differs per benchmark, requiring prior knowledge.

Absolute gains are modest in several settings: RoboCasa at 300 demos improves by only ~0.1-1.7 points; OpenVLA on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal actually decrease (85.2→81.7, 75.5→73.6); SIMPLER-WidowX average gains ~3.4 points. Success rates are averaged over 3 seeds but no variance/significance tests are reported, so several improvements may be within noise.

No comparison against trained-verifier baselines (e.g., value-function guidance from Nakamoto et al. 2024) in the same settings — the paper motivates the work by these methods' drawbacks but never demonstrates MG-Select is competitive with them in accuracy, only that it avoids their costs.

Limited technical depth/theoretical grounding: the choice of KL(Q||P) direction (reverse of the self-certainty KL(P||U) in Kang et al.) is not analyzed; the need for a large regularization temperature (τ=4.0) on the masked distribution and the 'First 5 tokens' aggregation heuristic are explained only post-hoc and speculatively.

Non-monotonic behavior in ablations (performance drops at N=8/16; peaks at τ=4.0) suggests the confidence signal is somewhat brittle, and the explanations remain hypotheses rather than validated analyses.

The joint training with condition dropout closely resembles classifier-free-guidance-style conditional/unconditional training; the novelty over such established techniques could be discussed more carefully.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: test-time scaling for VLAs without external verifiers, which is a meaningful simplification over verifier-based approaches (Nakamoto et al., Kwok et al.).

Broad empirical coverage spanning three simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO) and real-robot experiments, with multiple seeds and reasonably detailed ablations (inference strategy, number of candidates, masking variants, joint training, temperature, aggregation).
The single-prefill deployment analysis (45% latency reduction) is a practical engineering contribution that addresses the obvious compute overhead objection to Best-of-N for robots.
The paper is generally well written and the method is easy to follow, with a clear problem formulation and implementation details in the appendix.
The insight that likelihood-based selection fails due to over-concentrated fine-tuned distributions is plausible and motivates the uncertainty-aware reference distribution.
weaknesses: Serious methodological concern: hyperparameters (sampling temperature τ, number of candidates N, masking variant, and the unusual 'regularization temperature' for the reference distribution) are searched over large ranges per dataset and 'the best result for each policy' is reported (Appendix A.3). This is effectively test-set hyperparameter tuning, which inflates all reported gains and undermines the claimed generality.

The headline numbers are weaker than the framing suggests. On RoboCasa with 300 demos the gain is marginal (61.2→62.9 on All tasks; 43.2→46.9 on pick-and-place). The advertised '168% relative gain' comes from a base of only 5.3% → 14.2% success, which remains far below useful operating levels.

Results on LIBERO are mixed and inconsistent: with OpenVLA, LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal actually degrade (85.2→81.7 and 75.5→73.6), and gains over π0-FAST are small (92.0→93.1). This contradicts the claim of 'consistently' improving performance and suggests the method may not generalize.

Missing key baselines: the paper criticizes external verifiers for poor generalization and training cost, but never runs one (e.g., value-guided selection à la Nakamoto et al.) on the same benchmarks for a direct comparison. The comparison to verifier-free LLM approaches (uniform KL, likelihood) is included, but the margin over these simple baselines is often within noise (e.g., 30.0 vs 30.5 vs 31.0 PnP in Table 5a).

Several design choices appear post-hoc and task-specific rather than principled: aggregating only the first 5 tokens performs best 'inexplicably' (attributed speculatively to the FAST tokenizer), the reference distribution requires a high regularization temperature (τ=4.0) to work at all, and the optimal masking variant differs per benchmark and is chosen by search. This weakens the claim that condition-masking provides a general confidence signal.

The method requires retraining the VLA with condition-dropout data (joint training) to obtain meaningful gains (e.g., 17.0→31.0 PnP from Joint-IL alone in Table 5d), which contradicts the framing of a 'test-time' method requiring no additional training — the joint training is a substantive training-time intervention that changes the base policy.

The sensitivity to N is non-monotonic and noisy (Table 5b: 31.0 at N=4, 30.0 at N=8, 46.1 at N=16 on All), suggesting high variance and questionable test-time scaling behavior for a method whose premise is scaling inference compute.

Only autoregressive VLAs (π0-FAST, OpenVLA) are evaluated; applicability to the increasingly dominant diffusion/flow-based VLA family (π0, GR00T) is unaddressed, limiting the scope of the contribution.
Statistical rigor is limited: gains of 1–3 percentage points are reported with 3 seeds and no significance analysis, and some conclusions rest on differences well within plausible noise.
The OOD real-world evaluation involves only 2 tasks with 16 trials each, which is thin evidence for claims of improved zero-shot generalization.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated problem: removing the need for externally trained verifiers in VLA test-time scaling is valuable for deployment pipelines.

The condition-masking reference distribution is a sensible and somewhat creative way to construct an 'uncertainty-aware' baseline that remains aligned with the task distribution, and the joint training strategy with condition dropout is a reasonable mechanism to make the reference distribution well-behaved.

Broad empirical coverage: four distinct settings (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, real Franka robot), two base VLA architectures (π0-FAST, OpenVLA), demonstration-scale sweeps, and real in-distribution/OOD tasks.

Thorough ablation section covering sampling strategy, number of candidates, masking variants, joint training, temperature, and aggregation, plus a useful latency analysis with a single-prefill deployment variant.
weaknesses: Evaluation methodology concern: Appendix A.3 states that hyperparameters (sampling temperature τ, number of candidates N, masking variant, and regularization temperature over a 7-value range) are searched per dataset and the best result is reported. This effectively tunes on the test benchmark, inflating headline numbers. Without a held-out selection protocol or reporting across all configurations, the gains are difficult to trust at their stated magnitude.

Modest and inconsistent absolute gains relative to the framing: SIMPLER average improves 46.9→50.3, LIBERO with π0-FAST improves 92.0→93.1, RoboCasa 'All' at 300 demos is nearly flat (61.2→62.9). On LIBERO, some suites degrade (OpenVLA Spatial 85.2→81.7, Goal 75.5→73.6). The headline claims (28%, 35%, 168%) rest on small-trial real-world evaluations (16–24 trials) and on a low-data RoboCasa slice with low absolute success (5.3→14.2), where variance is high; no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are provided.

Limited novelty: the method is a fairly direct adaptation of verifier-free self-certainty Best-of-N selection (Kang et al., 2025) to VLAs, replacing the uniform reference with condition-masked distributions plus condition-dropout training. The main contributions are empirical; the 'First 5 tokens' aggregation and the need for a large regularization temperature (τ=4.0) suggest tokenizer-specific heuristics whose generalization to other VLAs/tokenizers is unclear.

No direct comparison against verifier-based test-time scaling baselines (e.g., value-function guidance or VLM verifiers) under matched compute/budget, which is the natural alternative the paper positions itself against; only weak ablation baselines (likelihood, uniform KL) are compared.

Sensitivity and brittleness: performance is non-monotonic in N (peak at N=4), aggregation choice changes results substantially, and several components work only in specific configurations, undermining the claim of a 'general test-time scaling paradigm'.

Some analysis is speculative (e.g., why first-5 aggregation works, why τ=4.0 regularizes the reference), and details of the single-prefill implementation are deferred to an appendix, limiting reproducibility of the efficiency claims.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned problem: verifier-free test-time scaling for VLAs avoids the training cost and generalization failures of external value-function verifiers (Nakamoto et al., Kwok et al.), which is a practically relevant contribution.

The core idea — using KL divergence from a condition-masked reference distribution of the same model as a confidence signal — is a simple, training-free selection mechanism that is a sensible adaptation of self-certainty ideas (Kang et al., 2025) to the VLA setting.

Comprehensive empirical coverage: three simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO), CALVIN for long-horizon tasks, real-robot experiments on Franka Research 3 with both ID and OOD tasks, and three base architectures (π0-FAST, OpenVLA, MiniVLA), demonstrating architectural generality.

Extensive ablations (N candidates, masking variants, sampling temperature, aggregation strategy, dropout ratio) plus a thoughtful analysis of the FAST tokenizer structure explaining why first-5-token truncation works (Appendix H).

Practical systems contribution: single-prefill deployment reduces latency substantially (e.g., 430s → 43.1s at N=64), and a direct comparison with RoboMonkey shows competitive accuracy at lower latency without an external verifier.
Honest reporting of limitations, including failure cases (Figure 4) and the observation that MG-Select without joint training yields only modest gains.
weaknesses: Hyperparameters are tuned per dataset/policy over wide ranges (τ, N, masking variant, regularization temperature ∈ {4.0–16.0}) and 'the best result for each policy' is reported — this effectively selects hyperparameters on the test environment, inflating headline numbers and weakening the evaluation's rigor. There is no held-out validation protocol.

Attribution of gains is muddled: Table 5(d) shows joint training alone improves PnP from 17.0 to 28.5, while adding MG-Select on top yields 31.0. Much of the headline improvement (e.g., the 168% relative gain) stems from the modified training procedure rather than the claimed test-time scaling mechanism, which weakens the central claim.

Absolute test-time-scaling gains are modest in several settings: RoboCasa 'All' at 300 demos is 61.2 → 61.3 without joint training; LIBERO averages improve by only 1.1 (π0-FAST) and 2.6 (OpenVLA) points; SIMPLER-WidowX is only reported with joint training. LIBERO-Goal actually degrades with MG-Select for both models.

Real-world results have small sample sizes (16–24 trials per task, 2 OOD tasks) with no variance or significance reporting in the main tables, so the 28%/35% relative gains carry substantial statistical uncertainty.

The method has considerable fragility requiring domain-specific tuning: aggregation that is optimal is 'First 5' on RoboCasa but 'First 1' on SIMPLER-WidowX, the best masking variant varies by benchmark, and the counterintuitive finding that highest-KL-from-reference = best action is only empirically motivated; the theoretical appendix (entropy monotonicity in temperature) is trivial and does not justify the selection rule.

Novelty is moderate: the framework is Best-of-N sampling with a KL-based confidence score adapted from LLM self-certainty work, combined with a condition-dropout fine-tuning strategy reminiscent of classifier-free guidance; the conceptual advance over Kang et al. (2025) applied to VLAs is incremental.

The regularization temperature of τ=4.0 on the reference distribution is an empirical patch for a poorly-behaved reference; the paper's explanation is speculative and the interaction between this temperature and the joint-training dropout is not analyzed.

strengths: The core idea of verifier-free test-time scaling via KL divergence from a condition-masking reference distribution is intuitive and addresses a real practical limitation of existing verifier-based approaches (training overhead and poor generalization).

Broad empirical coverage: three simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO), plus real-world Franka experiments in both in-distribution and OOD settings, with 3 random seeds and multiple base models (π0-FAST, OpenVLA, MiniVLA).

Thorough ablation studies (number of candidates, masking variants, joint training, regularization temperature, aggregation strategy) and an informative appendix, including a latency analysis and a single-prefill deployment trick that substantially reduces inference overhead.

The joint training strategy with condition dropout is a sensible mechanism for making the reference distribution meaningful, and the temperature-entropy derivation in Appendix E, while simple, is correct and supports the design choice.
Comparison against a recent verifier-based method (RoboMonkey) in Appendix D shows the method is competitive at lower latency without an external verifier.
weaknesses: Hyperparameters (masking variant, sampling temperature, regularization temperature, aggregation strategy) are searched per benchmark and the best configuration is reported (Appendix A.3). This is a form of test-set tuning that undermines the central claim of generalization and reliability; a held-out validation protocol or cross-dataset transfer of hyperparameters is needed to support the headline numbers.

Key design choices appear benchmark-specific and ad hoc: state-masking works best on SIMPLER but text-masking on RoboCasa; 'first 5 tokens' aggregation is best on RoboCasa while 'first 1' is best on SIMPLER (Table 12). The FAST-truncation analysis in Appendix H offers a hypothesis but no principled rule, weakening the claim that the method provides a 'reliable reference' in general.

Absolute gains are often modest and within plausible noise: RoboCasa at 300 demos improves 43.2→46.9 (PnP) and 61.2→62.9 (All); OpenVLA on LIBERO-Spatial/Goal actually slightly degrades. No statistical significance testing is reported despite success rates based on 24–50 trials.

In the direct comparison with RoboMonkey (Table 14), MG-Select is actually slightly worse on average (50.3 vs 50.7) and notably worse on the hardest task (13.9 vs 18.1), which weakens the 'external verifiers are unnecessary' narrative; the efficiency argument is stronger than the accuracy argument.

The high regularization temperature (τ=4.0) required to make the masked reference distribution usable is a somewhat troubling sign: the raw masked distribution underperforms even the uniform-KL baseline (Table 5e), suggesting the reference distribution does not behave as the conceptual motivation implies, and the 'peaked distribution' explanation is speculative.

Novelty is limited: the method is a fairly direct adaptation of self-certainty Best-of-N selection (Kang et al., 2025) to VLAs, with the main new ingredient being the condition-masking reference and a classifier-free-guidance-style dropout during fine-tuning, both of which are incremental.

Only autoregressive VLAs with discrete action tokens are covered; applicability to flow/diffusion-based VLAs (π0, GR00T N1), which are increasingly dominant, is unaddressed, limiting the scope of the claimed paradigm.

Some reporting is inconsistent (e.g., Table 2 shows only the MG-Select* variant while Table 3 shows the non-joint variant), and several strong statements (e.g., 'fundamentally limited', 'consistently improves') are stronger than the mixed evidence (e.g., failure cases in Figure 4, minor drops in LIBERO-Goal/Spatial).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: improving precision of autoregressive VLAs without training external verifiers, which is a meaningful departure from prior test-time scaling work (Nakamoto et al., Kwok et al.) that requires verifier training.

The core idea—using KL divergence from a condition-masking reference distribution as a verifier-free confidence signal—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly described, with an intuitive link to the model's internal uncertainty.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: RoboCasa (3 data regimes), SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO (two architectures), CALVIN, MiniVLA, and real-world ID/OOD tasks on a Franka arm, with comparisons to GR00T N1, RT-1-X, Octo, RoboVLM, SpatialVLA, and RoboMonkey (including latency).

Thorough ablations covering inference strategy, number of candidates, masking variants, joint training, regularization temperature, aggregation strategy, and dropout ratios, plus a latency-optimized single-prefill deployment and an analysis connecting FAST token truncation to reconstruction error.
Notable gains in the low-data regime (168% relative improvement on RoboCasa pick-and-place with 30 demos) and consistent real-world improvements (28% ID, 35% OOD), supported by qualitative rollouts.
The entropy-temperature analysis in Appendix E, while elementary, is correct and clarifies the design choice of the regularized reference distribution.
weaknesses: Per-dataset hyperparameter search over masking variant, sampling temperature, N, and regularization temperature, with best results reported per policy, raises concerns about evaluation selectivity and weakens the claim that the method is a plug-and-play, condition-agnostic framework; no principled guidance or validation set protocol is given for choosing these.

Gains are modest or marginal in several settings: RoboCasa 'All' at 300 demos improves only 61.2→61.3 without joint training, LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal slightly decrease, and the SIMPLER-WidowX improvement (46.9→50.3) is on top of a base model that already dominates other baselines, making the added value harder to gauge.

Novelty is incremental: Best-of-N with self-certainty/KL-based selection largely adapts existing LLM techniques (Kang et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2024) to VLAs; the main new component is the condition-masking reference distribution plus joint training, and the hypothesis about why masking provides a good reference is supported only empirically.

The aggregation strategy results are fragile and only partially explained: 'First 5' is best on RoboCasa but 'First 1' is best on SIMPLER-WidowX, and the FAST-tokenizer hypothesis is post-hoc; the design feels tuned to benchmarks rather than grounded in a principled account.

There is tension in the framing: the paper advertises 'no additional training,' yet the strongest results (MG-Select*) require a modified joint training (condition-dropout) procedure, which is an additional training-time change and complicates direct comparison to baselines trained with vanilla IL.

KL divergence is only computed against the single greedy-conditioned masking variant chosen per environment, and the theoretical justification for why higher-KL candidates are more precise is heuristic; no statistical significance tests are reported despite relatively small per-task trial counts (24–50 trials, 3 seeds).
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the many implementation details (dropout ratios, temperature values, token truncation choices).
